geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better preserves the intended 2D geometry: its circle panel is actually circular, the secant/tangent construction is laid out with consistent proportions, and it includes the rotational approach cue and intermediate secants. Figure 1 has a visibly distorted “circle” because of unequal x/y scaling, a more arbitrary wavy curve, and less complete structural indication of the secant rotating into the tangent.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2’s mode selector, distance slider, Q drag, and P drag all recompute the geometry and slope readouts consistently, with sensible minimum separations to avoid division-by-zero degeneracy. Figure 1’s panel buttons and dragging mostly work, but its Q slider is not a true distance-to-P control on the open curve and is especially incoherent on the circle because high slider values can wrap and clamp Q back near P; its animation also claims Q reaches P even though clampT prevents that and leaves the secant offset from the tangent.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the recognizable fan of purple secant lines converging to a tangent, includes the shaded/arrow indication of rotation, and has a blue curve with labeled P and Q in a composition similar to panel (a). Figure 1 has the axes and labeled points, but its curve shape is much less like the original, the secant/tangent construction is sparse and partly misplaced, and it omits the prominent shaded wedge and curved arrows that make the textbook figure recognizable.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the main mathematical labels P, Q, x, y, Tangent line, and Secant line at readable sizes and generally closer to the associated objects, whereas Figure 1’s plot labels are noticeably smaller and the tangent label is disconnected from the actual tangent construction. Figure 2’s tangent label is somewhat cluttered near the lower-left line and both figures include extra UI text not in the textbook, but Figure 1’s required labels are less legible and less well placed overall.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more accurately teaches the limiting definition: in both the smooth-curve and circle cases it keeps P and Q on the curve, draws the secant through P and Q, and shows it approaching the tangent as Q approaches P, matching the definition in the context and brief (L00007, L00010). Figure 1 gets the general idea, but its circle panel maps a mathematical circle with unequal x/y scales so the displayed object is an ellipse while still representing the construction as applying to a circle, weakening the intended confirmation that the limiting definition agrees with the classical tangent to a circle (L00007, L00010). Figure 1 also falsely asserts in its animation popup that Q has reached P and the secant coincides with the tangent even though its clamp prevents Q from actually reaching P, whereas the subject matter is a limiting process with Q different from P (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger across all dimensions: it preserves the circle/curve geometry more accurately, keeps P and Q on the curve, and clearly shows secants rotating toward the tangent with labels placed near the relevant objects. Figure 1 conveys the broad idea but is weaker because its circle is visibly distorted by unequal scaling, its secant-to-tangent construction is sparser and less faithful to the source, and some interactions/animation text incorrectly imply Q reaches P or that the slider represents a coherent distance control.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the textbook structure: it has a filled multiply connected region with distinct thick blue outer and inner boundaries, correct boundary-orientation arrowheads, well-placed C₁/C₂/R/R′/R″ labels, and a more faithful irregular outer contour with an off-center hole. Figure 2 is more schematic: the outer and inner curves are less proportionally faithful, the boundary arrows are drawn as generic V chevrons, the cut construction is less structurally clear, and the visible drag/resize dots add non-textbook marks inside the figure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested interactions more correctly: dragging or resizing the hole recomputes the filled region, C₂, orientation arrows, labels, and the panel (b) cuts, while the panel buttons animate the cuts growing in and out. Figure 2’s controls mostly work, but the panel toggle/step controls switch instantly rather than animating the cut introduction, and its cut geometry is a single horizontal level through the hole rather than the intended two horizontal cuts, so the advertised interaction is less faithful; its drag/resize constraints are also more ad hoc and less robust than Figure 1’s inside-region constraint.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the textbook panel because its outer region has the distinctive kidney-like indentation on the left and a more irregular inner hole, matching the overall geometry of the original better. Figure 1 uses the same colors and labels but its region is much more like a smooth oval blob, with a smaller simpler hole and less of the characteristic cut-in shape, so it reads less like the reference at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the required labels C1, C2, R, and (a) in readable italic styling with placements closer to the reference, especially C1 sitting cleanly above the outer boundary and C2 near the hole without collision. Figure 2 also includes the main labels, but its C1 label is crowded by and nearly overlaps the boundary/arrow at the top, making it less clean, and it adds a larger block of explanatory sidebar text that is not part of the original figure.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more accurately teaches the construction: it shows C1 counterclockwise and C2 clockwise, then uses two horizontal cut segments with paired opposite arrows on the same cuts, matching the cancellation of opposite line integrals along cuts and the division into R′ and R″ (L00007-L00014, L00056-L00057, L00072-L00073). Figure 1 gets the boundary orientations mostly right, but its panel (b) draws two horizontal levels that become four cut segments around the hole and gives each level only a single arrow direction, which can suggest different cuts cancel each other rather than each cut being traversed in opposite directions by the two subregion boundaries (L00013-L00014, L00056-L00057, L00073).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall submission because it more robustly implements the intended interactive behavior: dragging/resizing the hole updates the region, labels, orientations, and cut panels, and its controls animate the cut construction rather than switching abruptly as in Figure 2. It also has cleaner required labels and a clearer source-level boundary structure, whereas Figure 2 suffers from crowded labeling, extra non-textbook marks/sidebar text, and less faithful interaction behavior. Figure 2 is more recognizable visually and has a stronger conceptual depiction of cut cancellation, but those advantages are outweighed by Figure 1’s higher-confidence strengths in geometry, labels, and interactivity.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately reconstructs the shell geometry: the selected shell is an actual thick annular cylindrical sector spanning from x_{k-1} to x_k with height f(x_k*) and visible cutaway depth, whereas Figure 2 represents shells as zero-thickness open CylinderGeometry surfaces at the midpoint radius, so the Δx thickness is not geometrically present. Figure 1 also places the shell label on the shell surface and includes a clearer spatial relationship between the flat rectangle and its revolved 3D shell; Figure 2 shows all nested shell surfaces by default and lacks the cutaway/thickness structure, making the generated shell less faithful to the textbook geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s sliders consistently rebuild the selected rectangle and corresponding annular shell, update k when n changes, and keep the displayed radius, height, thickness, selected-shell volume, shell sum, and exact volume in sync with the drawn geometry. Figure 2’s k and n sliders mostly update highlights and values correctly, but its shells are zero-thickness cylindrical surfaces at the midpoint radius, so the n slider does not actually make the shells thinner as advertised; it only changes the number and spacing of surfaces while still reporting a finite thickness and volume.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because its right panel includes the translucent gray cylindrical volume with a cyan highlighted shell segment, matching the original composition much better. Figure 1’s shell is a dark, opaque standalone cylinder with a cutout and lacks the broad translucent outer cylinder context, so it reads less like the textbook figure despite having the same general shell-method idea.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the required main labels and captions more legible and less cramped than Figure 1, with clearer R_k, S_k, axis labels, panel labels, and caption text. Figure 1 includes similar labels, but they are noticeably smaller, more crowded around the left strip and shell, and harder to read at inline size; its extra sidebar annotations are also more visually dominant and distracting.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is conceptually more accurate because its selected rectangle spans x_{k-1} to x_k under a decreasing curve and its revolved object is a thick hollow annular shell with inner and outer radii corresponding to the strip boundaries, matching the idea that a thin vertical rectangle/strip revolved about the y-axis produces a cylindrical shell whose volume approximates the tube (L00007, L00010). Figure 2 gets the broad shell-method idea and labels mostly right, but its panel (b) shell is modeled as a zero-thickness open cylinder at the midpoint radius rather than a hollow cylindrical ring generated by the full rectangle thickness, so the displayed geometry contradicts the stated thickness Δx and is less faithful to the shell generated by the rectangle (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it represents the selected rectangle as a true thick annular cylindrical shell spanning the strip width and keeps its sliders, labels, and volume values synchronized with that geometry. Figure 2 has more legible labels and a rendered composition closer to the reference screenshot, but its shell is only a zero-thickness cylindrical surface at the midpoint radius, so its displayed geometry contradicts the stated Δx thickness and makes the n-slider/thickness behavior less conceptually and geometrically faithful.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook structure of the logistic sigmoid plot: it uses the boxed 0–1 by −5–5 frame with only the major tick labels, a thick orange sigmoid, centered fraction annotation, and the correct sig[z] and z axis labeling. Figure 2 reconstructs the same curve but adds many extra minor tick marks and gray guide crosshairs, places the formula inside the plot rather than centered near the top, and uses a more instructional step layout that makes the static structure less faithful to the original textbook figure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has more reliable interaction handlers: step changes, dragging, threshold updates, and resize all rerender the relevant dynamic elements using the current plot frame, and its drag coordinate conversion is based on the SVG bounds. Figure 1 directly exposes the intended controls and its threshold slider mostly works, but its drag mapping uses hard-coded 700×560 scaling and container padding rather than the actual SVG coordinate system, and its manually drawn guides/threshold endpoints are not recomputed on resize, so controls can become misaligned with what is drawn at non-default sizes.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is much more visually faithful to the reference: it preserves the simple black axes, orange sigmoid curve, grey dotted midpoint guides, formula placement, and overall plot composition. Figure 1 has the same basic sigmoid but adds prominent blue dashed guides, a black draggable point, explanatory labels, and a much smaller/shifted plotting area, making it read more like an annotated interactive widget than the original textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 better matches the original labels: it includes the formula, x-label z, y-label sig[z], and tick labels with clean placement and little clutter. Figure 1 adds invented interactive annotations on the plot that are not in the original, its y-label appears misplaced/duplicated outside the plotting area with a stray clipped character, and the extra blue threshold text crowds the central region.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly plot the logistic sigmoid formula as a monotone S-shaped curve over roughly z ∈ [−5,5] with axes labeled z and sig[z], and both correctly represent σ(0)=0.5 and the threshold/logit relationship in computation (L00007). Figure 2 is more conceptually accurate because its narration explicitly states the open interval (0,1), smooth asymptotic approach to both bounds, saturation behavior, and probability-threshold interpretation without introducing a misleading formula label (L00007). Figure 1 is mostly correct, but its on-plot threshold label writes ln(τ/1−τ), which is ambiguous or mathematically wrong compared with the intended ln(τ/(1−τ)), and both figures fail to show the requested dashed horizontal asymptote at sig[z]=1.0, so Figure 1 has the stronger conceptual blemish (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the stronger overall match because it is much closer visually and textually to the reference, preserving the simple axes, orange sigmoid, midpoint guides, formula, and clean z/sig[z] labeling, while Figure 1 adds prominent interactive annotations, blue threshold guides, a draggable point, and cluttered/misplaced labels that make it less faithful. Although Figure 1 better matches some static textbook-structure details and avoids Figure 2’s extra minor ticks/crosshairs, Figure 2’s interactions are more robust and its conceptual explanation is cleaner, whereas Figure 1 has resize/drag alignment issues and an ambiguous threshold-logit formula label.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 much better reconstructs the original multi-panel textbook structure: it includes the 3-by-2 layout with panels a)–f), the hidden-unit sequence including no-fit, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 50 units, consistent axes/ticks, seven training points, black true curve, and teal piecewise-linear fitted curves in each panel. Figure 2 collapses the figure into a single plot, omits the small-multiple layout and the no-fit panel, uses only six training points, substitutes sinusoidal/smoothed fits for several cases, and therefore loses much of the original topology, proportions, and comparative structure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested interactions much more correctly: clicking grid panels actually switches to a zoomed version of that configuration, the slider updates the displayed hidden-unit fit and title with animated curve transitions, and the 6-vs-50 toggle changes the active fitted curve. Figure 2's slider and overlay checkbox basically redraw correctly, but its 'Zoom to current panel' button only opens a popup rather than zooming, it has no clickable panel grid at all, and its contrast control overlays the 50-unit curve rather than toggling between the underfit and overfit panels.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original six-panel grid layout with panel labels, hidden-unit titles, repeated axes, black target curve, cyan fitted curves, and orange data points, making it recognizable as the same textbook figure at a glance. Figure 2 only shows a single enlarged 6-hidden-units panel and omits the broader multi-panel composition and panel labeling, so even though that one panel resembles part of the original, it is less recognizable as the full original figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 is much closer to the reference label set: it includes the six panel letters a)–f), the hidden-unit titles for the appropriate panels, and shared-style axis labels, whereas Figure 2 only shows a single '6 hidden units' panel and lacks the other panel labels/titles and the y-axis label. Figure 1's labels are somewhat small and the surrounding UI adds non-original text, but Figure 2 is far more incomplete relative to the original and also includes extra control labels not present in the textbook figure.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is more concept-accurate because it at least presents the requested six-panel comparison with the named hidden-unit counts 6, 7, 8, 10, and 50 and shows the intended qualitative trend that low hidden-unit fits are more oscillatory while the 50-unit fit is smoother (L00007-L00014). Figure 2 instead replaces the six-panel 3×2 figure with a single selectable plot, omits the additional configuration, and its narration says few hidden units merely produce a coarse underfit, which is a less faithful statement of the brief’s claim that decreasing hidden-unit count develops more oscillations and finer local structure (L00007-L00014).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger because it preserves the original six-panel 3×2 textbook structure with panel labels, hidden-unit titles, repeated axes, target curve, training points, and separate fitted curves, while Figure 2 collapses the material into a single selectable plot and omits much of the comparative layout. Figure 1 also implements the intended interactions more completely, with clickable panels, slider updates, and a 6-vs-50 toggle, whereas Figure 2’s zoom and contrast controls only partially approximate those behaviors. Figure 2 resembles one panel of the source, but it is much less faithful to the full figure and loses the intended comparison across hidden-unit counts.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the underlying MDP flow topology: it includes separate next-state and reward outputs from the environment, the current state and reward flowing to the agent, and both the state and action inputs returning to the environment with arrowheads. Figure 1 has more textbook-like colors and rounded-box styling, but structurally it omits or fails to connect the right-side state path, leaving the right 'State s_t' label essentially floating, and collapses several flows into only three main arrows.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s controls visibly and correctly update the intended elements: Agent clicks highlight the policy text and action arrow, Environment clicks highlight both transition and reward-function labels, and the animation steps through state, policy/action, and environment return highlights. Figure 2’s animation mostly works, but its click highlights for the policy and environment functions are drawn in a highlight group behind opaque boxes, making those advertised label highlights effectively invisible; the Agent click only visibly pulses the action line, and the Environment click provides little or no visible highlight of the requested functions. Figure 1 does have a flaw where interrupting an animation by clicking Agent/Environment can leave the animate button disabled, but its advertised interaction effects are otherwise more correct than Figure 2’s hidden highlights.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually recognizable as the textbook figure because the agent and environment boxes are larger, similarly placed, similarly colored, and retain the prominent rounded-box composition of the original. Figure 2 preserves some loop geometry more completely, but the whole diagram is much smaller, the boxes are flatter and less like the original proportions, and the added sidebar text dominates the screenshot, making it less faithful at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has noticeably larger and more readable diagram labels, with the Agent/Environment titles and internal policy/transition/reward annotations easier to read than in Figure 2. Figure 2 includes most of the same labels but the whole diagram is scaled down so many labels and formulas are too small for comfortable inline reading, while Figure 1’s main weakness is some crowding/overlap on the left labels such as Reward/State.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is conceptually more accurate because its labels and interaction text describe the agent as choosing/sampling an action according to the policy π[a_t|s_t] and the environment as governed by Pr(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) and Pr(r_{t+1}|s_t,a_t), matching the MDP loop described in the brief (L00007). Figure 2 also has the main probability labels correct, but its Agent popup says the policy determines the “best action” based on the current state, which falsely implies an optimal policy rather than merely selecting an action according to π as stated in the brief (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is overall stronger because it more closely matches the rendered textbook-style appearance, has larger and more readable labels, and its visible interactions correctly highlight the agent policy/action and environment transition/reward elements. Figure 2 does reconstruct the MDP flow topology more completely, with clearer separate state and reward returns, but it is visually smaller, its advertised click highlights are largely hidden behind opaque boxes, and its popup wording misleadingly implies the policy chooses the “best” action rather than sampling/selecting according to π.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the pinhole-projection geometry: O, the image plane, P, p, the solid projection ray, dashed displaced ray, and both velocity arrows are arranged in a coherent optical-axis layout with p actually lying on the O–P ray and on the plane. Figure 1 has the same general elements, but its geometry is less faithful: the image plane is a large filled z=0 square with O placed off-plane at z=3 and P behind it, the dashed displaced construction lacks a projected displaced image point, and its proportions/viewpoint feel more like a generic isometric schematic than the textbook camera-projection geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls recompute the projection and optical-flow vector using the correct perspective derivative, and its trajectory slider is a reasonable alternate affordance for moving P along the trajectory. Figure 2 has actual dragging, but the drag is constrained to a constant-depth plane rather than along the point's trajectory, and its optical-flow arrow/readout is based on a fairly large finite displacement rather than the instantaneous derivative, so the velocity-component sliders do not show the intended quantity as accurately.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable because it preserves the oblique image plane, the solid and dashed green rays diverging from O through the projected point toward P, and the basic spatial relationship of p on the plane and P beyond it. Figure 2 has the same elements but flattens the composition into an almost horizontal layout with a very narrow plane and nearly overlapping green lines, making it look less like the diagonal textbook diagram.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the required in-diagram labels O, p, ṗ, P, and Ṗ in clearer, larger, more readable positions, whereas Figure 2’s labels are much smaller, some are cramped near the geometry, and the P label is especially hard to read. Both figures include extra UI text not present in the original, but Figure 2 adds more explanatory/numeric annotations that clutter the labeling, while Figure 1’s scene labels more closely match the original overall.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents the projection ray from O through P to p and computes the 2D velocity as the actual time derivative of its perspective projection, matching the intended instantaneous relationship between Ṗ and ṗ (L00011-L00014, L00019). Figure 2 also shows a pinhole ray and projected point, but it uses the optical-axis coordinate as X with p = f·P/X while the brief establishes the perspective relations x = fX/Z and y = fY/Z with Z as depth (L00007-L00014, L00019), and its ṗ arrow is a finite-difference displacement over DT rather than the instantaneous derivative requested (L00011-L00014, L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it has clearer and more faithful labels and better represents the intended instantaneous perspective-projection relationship between the 3D point velocity and the image-plane velocity. Figure 2 has a more coherent source-code geometric layout in some respects, but relative to Figure 1 its labels are cramped, its visual composition is less like the rendered reference, and its interaction/optical-flow behavior relies on constrained dragging and finite displacement rather than the intended derivative.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the projective-geometry structure because it includes three distinct magenta transversals, four rays through O, four labeled point sets P, Q, and R with R1 handled at infinity, and it keeps the projected points constrained to their corresponding lines. Figure 2 omits the P transversal entirely, places the P points only approximately collinear, and its dragging model can further break the required collinearity, so the node/line topology and geometric proportions are less faithful despite having a similar overall concept.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested interactive handlers much more completely: P, Q, R, and O can all be dragged, and each drag recomputes the associated ray intersections and updates the displayed cross-ratio in real time. Figure 2 only supports dragging P points and O, not Q or R, and its P drag moves points along individual rays rather than along a common collinear line, so Q/R often do not change with the P motion and the displayed cross-ratios are not a correct demonstration of invariance; its P set is not even consistently treated as collinear. Figure 1 is not perfect because it forces the three displayed cross-ratio values to be the same ray-based value rather than independently recomputing each set, but its controls behave far closer to the intended projection interaction than Figure 2.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the original composition with four rays from O, three magenta transversal lines, labeled P/Q/R point families, and the R1→∞ indication. Figure 2 captures the rough ray-and-transversal geometry, but its labels are reduced to repeated numbers, it omits the prominent P/Q/R notation and infinity arrow, and overall reads less like the textbook figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 is much closer to the original labeling, with O and the P_i, Q_i, and R_i labels including R_1→∞ placed near the corresponding points, whereas Figure 2 mostly replaces these with bare numbers 1–4 and omits the crucial P/Q/R distinctions on the diagram. Figure 1’s labels are small and somewhat crowded around P_2–P_4, and it includes extra sidebar text, but Figure 2’s diagram labels are far less complete and more ambiguous, with several tiny numeric labels that do not match the textbook annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the required projective setup: P, Q, and R are each constrained to collinear transversals, rays from O relate corresponding points, and R1 is placed at infinity exactly when the R line is parallel to the OP1Q1 ray, matching the brief (L00007-L00010). Figure 2 correctly makes the R line parallel to the first ray so R1 is at infinity, but its P points are not collinear and it still labels/computes a CR(P) by projecting those non-collinear points onto a direction, which makes its claim that the cross-ratio of each set stays identical conceptually false for the stated subject matter (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger because it preserves the projective configuration with four rays from O, three distinct transversals, collinear P/Q/R point sets, and the R1→∞ condition, while Figure 2 omits the P transversal and allows or displays P points in ways that break the required collinearity. Figure 1 also implements substantially more of the intended interaction, allowing P, Q, R, and O dragging with recomputation, whereas Figure 2 only supports a narrower set of drags and can make the cross-ratio demonstration conceptually incorrect. Visually and textually, Figure 1 keeps the original P_i/Q_i/R_i labeling and infinity annotation, while Figure 2’s mostly numeric labels are less faithful and more ambiguous.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better reconstructs the core 3D pinhole-camera geometry because it uses full vertical planes for the wall and barrier with a genuinely circular aperture and places the scene object, barrier, and image wall along a clear optical axis. Figure 1 has a more complete set of ray lines, but its “pinhole” barrier is geometrically a horizontal slit made from only top and bottom slabs, not a point/circular aperture, and its inverted image is only a few sample blobs rather than a fuller projected object.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls consistently update the advertised state: the pinhole toggle fades from mixed wall rays to barrier-restricted rays and an inverted image, the comparison toggle correctly brightens many rays to one wall point without the pinhole and only the corresponding pinhole ray with the aperture, and the size slider changes both the gap and blur in the expected direction across its range. Figure 2's controls mostly redraw, but its pinhole comparison is less correct because the highlighted-wall-location mode draws extra solid rays that stop at arbitrary barrier intersections rather than cleanly showing the one wall-reaching ray through the pinhole, and its mode switch is a hard radio redraw rather than the requested linked transformation.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook diagram because it preserves the key composition of a wall on the left, a tree on the right, and multiple green/brown light rays between them. Figure 2 instead places the tree in front of a large gray plane, loses the clear wall-at-left geometry and ray structure, and overall reads more like a generic 3D scene than the original optical diagram.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the key labels “Wall” and “Pinhole” large and readable near the corresponding elements, whereas Figure 2’s diagram labels are extremely tiny, low-contrast, and hard to read. Figure 1 does add non-original clutter such as “Tree (scene)” and UI/caption text, but Figure 2 is worse because the relevant textbook-style annotations are essentially illegible and poorly placed.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 is conceptually more accurate overall: its no-aperture state shows different tree points sending rays to the same wall locations, and its pinhole state uses an opaque barrier with a genuinely localized circular hole plus an inverted wall image, matching the contrast between no coherent image and aperture-restricted one-to-one projection (L00007-L00010). Figure 1 has strong ray mapping and an inverted projection, but it undermines the key mechanism by constructing the barrier as two slabs with a long slit-like gap rather than a single pinhole, and it leaves a visible “Pinhole” label even in the no-aperture state, falsely suggesting the aperture exists in panel (a) (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall result because it more faithfully resembles the intended textbook-style wall/tree/ray diagram, has readable key labels, and its interactive controls behave more consistently than Figure 2’s. Figure 2 has a more geometrically and conceptually correct circular pinhole/barrier, but relative to Figure 1 it loses the recognizable composition, makes its annotations nearly illegible, and its highlighted-ray interaction introduces confusing extra rays rather than cleanly showing the intended pinhole mapping.
